安.note: A woman sheltered under a roof — in ancient China this image embodied total peace and security for the household. The character captures the idea that safety begins at home.

明.note: Sun and moon together — the two great sources of natural light. Their union creates the concept of brightness, clarity, and understanding itself.

好.note: A woman beside a child — the ancient image of goodness, harmony, and completion. Some scholars also read it as the joy of new life.

休.note: A person leaning against a tree — the universal image of rest. This pictographic logic has been unchanged for over three thousand years.

男.note: Strength applied to the field. In the agrarian civilization of ancient China, a man was defined by his labour in the paddy fields — the character encodes this social role directly.

radicals.meaning: the character itself is a radical

木.note: One of the oldest pictographs — a tree with roots below and branches above. The radical 木 seeds hundreds of characters related to trees, wood, and growth.

radicals.meaning: the character itself is a radical

日.note: Originally drawn as a circle with a dot — the sun and its core. The dot distinguishes it from 口 (mouth). 日 seeds all characters related to time, light, and heat.

radicals.meaning: the character itself is a radical

月.note: The crescent moon — one of the most stable pictographs in Chinese. 月 also doubles as the radical for 肉 (flesh/meat), leading to many body-part characters.

radicals.meaning: the character itself is a radical

山.note: Three mountain peaks rendered as brushstrokes — a direct sketch of the landscape. 山 appears in place names, nature poetry, and spiritual concepts of stillness and permanence.

radicals.meaning: the character itself is a radical

水.note: Flowing water shown as a central current with side streams. As the radical 氵 it influences hundreds of characters related to rivers, liquids, and states of flow.

radicals.meaning: the character itself is a radical

火.note: Flames rising — a direct pictograph of fire. As a radical (灬 or 火) it appears in characters for cooking, heat, light, and passion.

学.note: A child under a sheltering structure — learning happens in a protected space, nurtured and guided. The traditional form 學 includes hands passing knowledge downward.

radicals.meaning: the character itself is a radical

人.note: A standing person seen from the side, legs apart. One of the oldest and most productive pictographs — 人 or 亻 appears in countless characters involving human beings, roles, and relationships.

radicals.meaning: the character itself is a radical

大.note: A person with arms spread wide — embodying largeness, greatness, and abundance. The same figure with a dot above becomes 天 (sky/heaven), and a dot below becomes 太 (great/excessive).

radicals.meaning: the character itself is a radical

心.note: A pictograph of the physical heart — in Chinese philosophy the heart is also the seat of mind, emotion, and consciousness. As radical 忄 it seeds all characters involving feeling and thought.

radicals.meaning: the character itself is a radical

口.note: An open mouth — simple, direct, and enormously productive. 口 appears in characters for speaking, eating, singing, and calling. It also represents openings, gates, and entrances by extension.

时.note: The sun measured in small increments — time itself. The traditional form 時 pairs 日 with 寺 (temple), a place where time was marked by bells. The simplified form keeps the essence.

友.note: Two right hands reaching toward each other — a handshake across time. Friendship in the oracle bone script was literally two hands meeting. The gesture defines the relationship.

国.note: A treasure (jade, or a weapon in older forms) enclosed within a border — a nation is defined by what it protects within its boundaries. The simplified form uses 玉 (jade), the most precious material in Chinese civilization.

radicals.meaning: the character itself is a radical

中.note: A vertical line piercing the center of a rectangle — an arrow hitting the bullseye. 中 means middle, center, and China itself (中国, the Middle Kingdom), the country that considered itself the center of the world.

我.note: Originally a pictograph of a halberd — a serrated battle-axe on a pole. The left side resembles 手 (hand) but is actually the weapon's handle; the right side is 戈, the serrated blade. The pronunciation was borrowed (假借 jiǎjiè) to write the word for 'I', and the weapon meaning was completely forgotten. The 戈 radical survives in 战 (war), 武 (military), and 戒 (caution) — reminders of the origin. Every time a Chinese speaker says 我, they are etymologically holding an ancient battle axe.

radicals.meaning: the character itself is a radical

了.note: One of the simplest strokes in the script — a single curved hook. The oracle bone form 𠃌 is thought to depict a swaddled infant, arms bound at the sides: something tightly wrapped, finished, complete. From this image grew the word liǎo — to finish, to end, to settle. Over time the same character was borrowed as the grammatical particle le, placed after a verb to mark a completed action. The same tiny hook that once pictured a bundled child now signals, thousands of years later, that something is done.

会.note: The oracle bone form 會 shows a lid sealed over a vessel with steam rising from below — the image of a pot brought together at the top. From this concrete picture of closing and containing, the meaning expanded outward: things gathering → people assembling → 开会, to hold a meeting. Then a further leap: gathering implies readiness and capability, so 会 also came to mean 'can' or 'be able to' — to have the skill or means for something. One character, one lid on a steaming pot, and from it grew assembly, skill, and possibility.

他.note: 亻(person) + 也 (phonetic). The twist: 他 was never originally a pronoun. The character 佗 (tuó) meant 'other, different' — hence 他人 (other people) — while 他 itself had a rather different, unflattering meaning in the Shuowen Jiezi. The character was borrowed (假借, jiǎjiè) as a sound-loan for the 3rd person pronoun, the same technique used for 我 and 了 — ancient Chinese frequently hijacked existing characters for new grammatical words. Before this, classical Chinese used 彼 (bǐ), 其 (qí), and 伊 (yī) for he/she. The modern three-way split — 他 (he), 她 (she), 它 (it) — was invented by poet and linguist 刘半农 (Liu Bannong) in the 1920s, barely a century ago. Memory hook: 亻+ 也 = 'person… also' → 'that other person' → 'he'.

怎.note: 乍 (zhà) originally depicted something sudden — like a person abruptly stopping — paired with 心 (heart). The combination asks: "What suddenly hits the heart?" → "How could this be?!" → "How / Why?" So 怎 is literally asking your heart about something sudden — capturing surprise, confusion, and bewilderment in a single character. Every time you ask 怎样? (how is it?), you're invoking an ancient picture of sudden shock hitting the heart.

么.note: 么 is the simplified form of 麼. In many languages, question words come from words meaning 'small/tiny' (think English 'what' from 'hwæt'). 幺 means 'tiny,' and 麼 was borrowed for its sound to become a question tag. So 么 by itself means nothing — it's just a question marker, like a '?' in speech. When you add 么 to the end of a statement, you're borrowing an ancient word for 'tiny' to transform that sentence into a gentle, colloquial question.

radicals.meaning: speech / words — a mouth with sound coming out
exchange — two people facing each other exchanging something

说.note: 言 (mouth with speech rising from it) + 兌 (two people facing each other, exchanging). Speaking is literally the exchange of words. The same 兌 radical seeds 悦 (yuè = joyful — an exchange that pleases the heart) and 税/稅 (shuì = tax — your exchange with the state). 说 itself has two readings: shuō (everyday speech) and the classical shuì (to persuade, as in 游说 — to travel and convince). In Confucianism, 言 carries enormous moral weight — 言而有信, 'let your words be trustworthy,' is one of the cardinal virtues. Every time you say 说, you invoke a 3,000-year-old image of two people exchanging breath and meaning across a threshold.

radicals.meaning: person — the human radical (亻= 人 leaning left)
abruptly begin; pictograph of cutting cloth (labor)

做.note: 乍 is the heart of 做 — a 3,000-year-old pictograph of a person cutting cloth: someone in the act of labor. It evolved into 作 (classical: to rise up and begin work), then the folk script added another 亻 to make 做, emphasizing who is doing the action. 做 handles concrete, everyday tasks (做饭 = cook, 做梦 = dream); its twin 作 survives in literary contexts (作品 = artwork, 作文 = composition). In speech they are nearly interchangeable, but 做人 — how you conduct yourself as a human being — remains one of the most distinctly Confucian phrases in the language.

radicals.meaning: from 物 (wù) — thing (now just a suffix)

什么.note: 什么 began life as two full words: 甚 (shén, 'what/which') + 物 (wù, 'thing'). Literally: 'what thing?' Over centuries of spoken erosion, 甚物 → 甚麼 → 什么, the full word 物 shrinking to the light suffix 么. The same compression happens in English: 'what thing' → 'what.' Today 么 by itself has no independent meaning — it exists only as a grammatical echo of the thing it once named. So every time you ask 你吃什么？you are asking 'you eat what-thing?' — a fossil of a full sentence compressed into two syllables by a thousand years of fast speech.

哪.note: 哪 is NEVER used alone in speech — always pairs with 里/个/天/儿. The radical breakdown tells the story: 口 (mouth) + 那 (that one). In ancient Chinese, you would point 你的手 (your hand) at something and ask with your 口 mouth: 'THAT one?!' The original character was just 那 (that), but when spoken as a QUESTION word, speakers added 口 to mark the pragmatic shift: from declarative 'that' to interrogative 'which that?' Over centuries, the new form 哪 took over the interrogative function entirely. Today 那 (that) and 哪 (which) are sharply split by speech act, not etymology. The character encodes a crucial insight: in Chinese, asking requires the mouth to be explicitly present. Memory hook: QUESTION MARK is MOUTH shape 👄 asking 'which?'

compounds.meaning: have been to (went and came back)
to pass away (euphemism: leave the world)

去.note: 去 is one of the ancient four directional verbs (来 lái come, 去 qù go, 往 wǎng go-to, 还 huán return-to). The pictograph is startling in its directness: 大 (person) standing at a door, taking the step OUT — that physical motion is 'to go.' But 去 also means 'past' and 'previous' because in Chinese temporal logic, the past is the direction you WENT (and left behind). 去年 (qùnián) = 'the year that went away.' 去 is the character that embodies motion away, passage of time, and farewell in one form. A 3,000-year-old picture of walking out a door still shapes every Chinese temporal reference.
去.etymology: Radical breakdown: 大 (person) over 厶 (departing self). The original oracle bone form shows a person inside a 囗 (enclosure = home) with strokes indicating departure. The modern simplified form keeps the essence: top = person, bottom = the private self in motion away. This is why 去 can mean both physical departure and temporal pastness — they're the same trajectory through space-time.

听.note: The traditional form 聽 reveals the philosophy: 耳 (ear) + 悳 (virtue/heart) + 直 (straight) + 心 (heart). Later simplified to 聽 with 耳 (ear) + 德 (virtue) + 心 (heart), then to modern 听 with 耳 + 口 + 斤. But the core truth remains: true listening in Chinese philosophy is NOT just hearing. It's ear + mouth + heart + effort all engaged together. The famous Confucian concept: 听而后言 (listen first, then speak), captures the moral weight. In Qi Gong 氣功, '用心听' (listening with your heart) means sensing qi/energy, not just sound. Your 心 heart is the REAL ear. This is why 听话 doesn't just mean 'obedient' — it means your ear, heart, and effort are all aligned with what's being said. Mencius: 耳不聪目不明 'If ears don't listen with the whole being, eyes don't see clearly' — all senses start from the 心 heart.
听.etymology: The traditional character 聽 breaks down: 耳 (ear, physical hearing) + 悳 (virtue, suggesting moral/emotional dimension) + 直 (straight/direct) + 心 (heart). The simplified form 听 keeps just 耳 (ear) + 口 (mouth) + 斤 (effort). But both versions encode the same truth: listening involves the physical ear, social context (the mouth/speaker), and dedicated effort. It's never passive.
